gap: None of the results ChatGPT got works out what a NAS costs to run each year, or how long it takes to pay for itself against Google One. On makers' power figures and the EIA's August 2026 US residential rate of 18.16 ¢/kWh, an always-on DS225+ costs about $27 a year, a DS425+ about $45 and a DXP2800 about $26. Google One's 2 TB plan costs $119.88 a year. Against that plan, the $389.99 DXP2800 enclosure (drives not included) pays for itself in about 4.2 years.
standout_why: I checked three pages. Our current page has Backblaze B2 at $6.95/TB a month and the size of a 100k-photo library, but no watts, power cost or Google One break-even. homelabcompass.com (cited) has no figures at all: no power, no cost per TB, no break-even. esp32.co.uk (cited) has only one example: a 25 W mini PC using 219 kWh a year, with no dollar figure, no real product and no Google One comparison. ChatGPT's own answers give enclosure prices but never running cost or payback.
decides: This backs the 2-bay pick over the 4-bay one for most families. The DS425+ draws 28.25 W when accessed against 16.98 W for the DS225+, so it costs about $18 more a year to run on top of its higher price. The DS225+ and DXP2800 cost about the same to run ($27 vs $26 a year), so running cost doesn't separate them. The payback figure answers the question the shopper is really asking ('is replacing Google Photos worth it?'): the enclosure alone takes about 4 years against the 2 TB plan, and under 2 years against the 5 TB plan ($239.88/yr), which a family library over 2 TB would need. Drives are left out because I couldn't source a drive price, so real payback is longer.
